paper.title: From Native Memes to Global Moderation: Cross-Cultural Evaluation of Vision–Language Models for Hateful Meme Detection
paper.abstract: Cultural context profoundly shapes how people interpret online content, yet vision–language models (VLMs) remain predominantly trained through Western or English-centric lenses. This limits their fairness and cross-cultural robustness in tasks like hateful meme detection. We introduce a systematic evaluation framework designed to diagnose and quantify the cross-cultural robustness of state-of-the-art VLMs across multilingual meme datasets, analyzing three axes: (i) learning strategy (zero-shot vs. one-shot), (ii) prompting language (native vs. English), and (iii) translation effects on meaning and detection. Results show that the common ''translate-then-detect'' approach deteriorate performance, while culturally aligned interventions — native-language prompting and one-shot learning — significantly enhance detection. Our findings reveal systematic convergence toward Western safety norms and provide actionable strategies to mitigate such bias, guiding the design of globally robust multimodal moderation systems.
